placeExistsBasis: WebSearch confirmed: Hiddenite is a census-designated place in east-central Alexander County, North Carolina (pop. 507, 2020 census), on NC Hwy 90 ~5 mi east of Taylorsville and ~15 mi NW of Statesville. Named for mineralogist William Earl Hidden (1853-1918), who discovered the green spodumene gem 'hiddenite' there in 1879 while prospecting platinum for Thomas Edison. Home of Emerald Hollow Mine. A genuine, specific, single US place. Strong on existence.

winks.verdict: KILL (as a distinct entity); the underlying observation is real but it is ONE entity, not three
winks.reason: Plain reading is strong: the word literally contains 'Hidden', the natural word for a concealed treasure, AND is an exact real NC place. As a single wink this is legitimate and not a cipher. BUT this is the same noun 'Hiddenite' that the other two winks also cite. It is one concept counted three times across three pages, not three distinct entities winking independently.

winks.verdict: KILL as distinct entity (duplicate of wink 1)
winks.reason: Identical claim to wink 1 with the county appended. Same word 'Hiddenite' on a different page. No new independent entity is winking; this is the noun repeated. Counting it separately inflates distinctEntities.

winks.verdict: KILL as distinct entity (duplicate of wink 1)
winks.reason: Again the same word 'Hiddenite'. Plain-language and real, but it is the third restatement of one concept, not a third independent entity.

criticalFlaw: All three 'supporting' winks are the SAME noun -- 'Hiddenite' -- appearing on three book pages. The wordplay test is supposed to count DISTINCT entities winking at a location (e.g. for Alexander: Alexander Calder, Antiquities of Alexander, Alexander the Great -- genuinely different nouns). Hiddenite has only ONE entity ('Hiddenite' itself) repeated. Distinct surviving entities = 1, not 3.
strengthOfTheOneSurvivingWink: The single surviving wink is genuinely strong: 'Hidden'+'ite' is a vivid, plain-language nod to a hidden treasure, it is a real and specific NC place, it sits in Alexander County (the book's top-scoring location and a chapter title 'Antiquities of Alexander'), and the gem's discovery story ties to a chapter object. As ONE clue it is among the best in the whole map. But one strong clue is not a wordplay HUB.
survivingEntitiesBasis: After collapsing the three duplicate citations of the single noun 'Hiddenite' into one entity, exactly one distinct entity winks at this place. It survives refutation (plain, non-cipher, location-specific, not generic) but it is alone.
isRivalBasis: A serious rival requires >=3 DISTINCT surviving entities. Hiddenite has only 1 distinct entity (the word 'Hiddenite' itself, cited thrice). It fails the multiplicity test. It is a single excellent clue, not an independent convergence hub. Notably its strength derives from being IN Alexander County -- it reinforces the Alexander cluster rather than standing as a separate rival.
verdict: Real, specific NC place with one genuinely strong plain-language wink ('Hidden'+ite). But its 3 'entities' are the same noun repeated; only 1 distinct entity -> not a rival hub.
